# Bus Driver's Heroic Escape Earns Him Hero Status in Pakistan

LAHORE, Pakistan (CNN) -- Driving a bus was simply his profession. Yet today, Meher Mohammad Khalil stands celebrated as someone who saved numerous lives. This Wednesday, he returned to the site where armed attackers had targeted his vehicle just a day earlier.

The assault occurred Tuesday when attackers emerged suddenly from concealed positions, firing at the bus transporting Sri Lanka's cricket squad. In that critical moment, Khalil assessed the danger and managed to bring his passengers through unharmed.

Speaking with CNN on Wednesday, Khalil recounted: "Initially, I mistook the gunfire for fireworks exploding. But witnessing the security vehicles ahead of us come under attack left me completely speechless."

He continued, explaining how another security vehicle provided cover, which restored his composure. "Seeing that protection gave me back my nerve and resolve. I made up my mind to get the vehicle out of there—regardless of any obstacle in my path, even if it meant driving over someone, I was determined to get that bus away safely."

Khalil made his way back to the attack site in Lahore on Wednesday, bringing flowers to honor those who lost their lives. Among the deceased was his colleague and friend, Zafar Khan, another bus driver whose vehicle had trailed behind Khalil's during the convoy.

"Tears welled up thinking about how these were men I'd shared meals with, who lost their lives simply performing their jobs," Khalil reflected.

The convoy had been en route to Gaddafi Stadium, where Sri Lanka's cricket team planned to resume their match against Pakistan. The violence claimed six police officers' lives along with Khalil's friend Khan, who had been driving the bus carrying match officials.

Members of the Sri Lankan cricket squad credited Khalil's rapid decision-making with saving their lives, though six players sustained injuries from flying glass and shrapnel. Team captain Mahela Jayawardene posted a tribute on his website, stating that Khalil "likely saved our lives, displaying extraordinary courage as he continued driving despite being directly fired upon."

When Khalil visited the location where everything had changed for him so suddenly, crowds gathered around him. One onlooker declared, "He's truly a hero—a genuine hero, a real champion of ordinary people."

Anonymous benefactors from Lahore presented Khalil with 300,000 rupees (exceeding $3,000)—a substantial sum for someone in his profession.

Despite the recognition, Khalil says grief remains his dominant emotion over the lives lost. He appealed directly to those responsible for the attack, urging them to remember that their targets were fellow human beings with families—mothers and sisters of their own.

"In God's name, I beg you to end this terrorism and give our nation some peace," he pleaded.

*CNN's Zein Basravi contributed to this report.*

Umpire Ahsan Raza, who was traveling in a separate vehicle, was critically wounded in the attack, having been shot at close range. Several Sri Lankan players — including Thilan Samaraweera, Tharanga Paranavitana, and the team's assistant coach Paul Farbrace — suffered injuries from bullets and shrapnel, though none proved life-threatening.

## The Bus Driver's Split-Second Heroism

Amid the terror, one man's composure and courage have emerged as a defining story of the attack: bus driver Mohammad Khalil.

As gunmen closed in and fired directly at the vehicle, Khalil refused to stop or reverse — a decision that many officials and survivors credit with saving the lives of everyone aboard. Despite the windows shattering around him and bullets striking the bus, Khalil kept his foot on the accelerator, driving directly through the assault and onto the stadium grounds, where the team could be secured.

"He didn't panic. If he had stopped even for a second, I don't want to imagine what would have happened," said a team security official who was present at the scene. "He drove that bus like his life — and everyone else's — depended on it, because it did."

Khalil later told reporters he had no time to think, only to act. "I just wanted to get them to safety. I have never experienced anything like this, but stopping was not an option in my mind."

His actions have been widely hailed as heroic, with cricket boards, players, and Pakistani officials publicly praising his bravery in the days following the attack.

## Nation and Cricketing World React with Grief and Anger

The attack has drawn swift condemnation from governments and cricketing bodies around the world. Pakistan's president and prime minister both issued statements expressing sorrow over the loss of police officers who died shielding the visiting team, and vowed that those responsible would be brought to justice.

"This was not just an attack on cricketers — it was an attack on Pakistan itself, on our hospitality, our spirit, and our future," said one senior Pakistani official. "We will not allow terrorism to define who we are as a nation."

Sri Lankan cricket officials expressed relief that their players survived but voiced anguish over the incident, which has once again cast a shadow over international cricket's willingness to tour Pakistan. Several nations had already been hesitant to send teams following prior security concerns, and this attack is expected to deepen that reluctance for years to come.

Cricketing legends and former players from around the world took to the media to condemn the violence. "Sport is supposed to be a unifying force, a symbol of hope," said one former international captain. "To see it targeted this way is a tragedy not just for Pakistan, but for the game we all love."

## A City in Mourning, A Call for Unity

In the aftermath, vigils were held across Lahore for the slain police officers, several of whom were recognized for shielding players and officials with their own bodies during the assault. Their sacrifice, officials say, prevented what could have been a far deadlier outcome.

Local citizens, many of them visibly shaken, expressed a mixture of grief, anger, and resolve in interviews conducted throughout the day.

"We are tired of this," said Fatima Rashid, a Lahore resident who came to lay flowers near the site of the attack. "Enough blood has been spilled. We want the world to know that this is not who we are. These terrorists do not represent Pakistan or Islam. They represent hatred, and hatred must be defeated."

Civil society groups and religious leaders alike issued statements calling for unity against extremism, urging the international community not to abandon Pakistan in its fight against terror, but instead to stand with its people.

"This attack was meant to isolate us, to make the world turn away," said a local community organizer. "Instead, it must be a moment that brings us together — Pakistanis, and the entire world — in a shared commitment to end this cycle of violence once and for all."

As investigations continue into the identities and motives of the attackers, Lahore remains under heightened security, with residents and officials alike vowing that the attack will not be allowed to define the city's legacy or its future relationship with the sport it so deeply loves.
